title: Hackers With Root Access Can Hijack SPIFFE Identities on Kubernetes Nodes
content_md: Security researchers have demonstrated how attackers with root-level access to a Kubernetes node could impersonate workloads and obtain their machine identities in SPIFFE/SPIRE environments. The research, published by Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, shows that an attacker who has already compromised a node can manipulate Linux control group, or cgroup, information used during workload attestation. This could trick a SPIRE agent into issuing SPIFFE Verifiable Identity Documents (SVIDs) belonging to other workloads running on the same node. Unit 42 said it has not observed this technique being exploited in real-world attacks. However, the findings underline a major cloud-native security concern: once an attacker gains root access to a node, the trust boundary protecting identities on that host can collapse. SPIFFE, short for Secure Production Identity Framework for Everyone, is an open standard for workload identity. Its reference implementation, SPIRE, is widely used in Kubernetes and cloud environments to replace long-lived passwords, API keys, and certificates with short-lived cryptographic credentials. Root Access Threatens SPIFFE SPIFFE gives each workload a unique SPIFFE ID, while an SVID acts as the proof that the workload owns that identity. SVIDs can be issued as X.509 certificates for mutual TLS authentication or as JSON Web Tokens for application authorization. In a normal SPIRE deployment, a workload requests its identity from the SPIRE agent running locally on the node
